Parallel and High-Throughput Topic Modeling

Source: vignettes/articles/parallel.Rmd
parallel.Rmd

A topic model in sbert is built in three stages:

  1. Encode: each text becomes an embedding, computed by the ONNX model.
  2. Tokenize: each text is split into words, which label the topics and measure their coherence.
  3. Cluster: the embeddings are grouped into topics by k-means.

Encoding takes far longer than the other two stages. A large corpus is therefore fast to model mainly when it is encoded as few times as possible. This article shows how, in order of how much time each step saves:

  1. Encode a corpus once and reuse the result, within a session and across sessions.
  2. Use several processor cores and threads.
  3. Avoid wasted work when encoding sentences.

None of these steps changes the topics, except three settings that are flagged below.

Only the last code chunk runs when this article is built. The others need a downloaded model, so they are shown but not run. They use the covid abstracts that ship with the package:

abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")

Encode once, fit many times

topics() and compare_topics() encode the text themselves. If you fit several models to the same corpus, encode it once with encode() and pass the result as embeddings:

embeddings <- encode(abstracts$Abstract)

model_8 <- topics(abstracts$Abstract, n_topics = 8, embeddings = embeddings)
model_12 <- topics(abstracts$Abstract, n_topics = 12, embeddings = embeddings)

topic_corpus() goes one step further. It stores both the embeddings and the tokenized words, so later fits repeat neither:

prepared <- topic_corpus(abstracts$Abstract, embeddings = embeddings)

sweep <- compare_topics(prepared, n_topics = c(6, 8, 10, 12))
model_8 <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 8)

compare_topics() already prepares the corpus once for all the counts it compares. A topic_corpus() object is useful when you run several sweeps, or your own loop, on the same text.

Reuse embeddings across sessions

encode(cache = ) saves embeddings to a file and reads them back the next time. Each text is stored under a SHA-256 digest of the text and the model’s settings, so only texts that are not yet in the file are encoded:

store <- file.path(tools::R_user_dir("sbert", "cache"), "covid_embeddings.rds")

embeddings <- encode(abstracts$Abstract, cache = store)  # encodes everything
embeddings <- encode(abstracts$Abstract, cache = store)  # encodes nothing

Because each text has its own entry, the cache also works when the corpus changes. If you correct some abstracts, add new ones, reorder the rows, or take a subset, only the new or changed texts are encoded. Repeated texts are encoded once per call.

The digest covers the text exactly as the model sees it (including any prefix) and the model’s name, revision, dimension, maximum length, pooling, and normalize. Change any of these and the texts are encoded again; a different model never reuses another model’s embeddings.

batch_size and sort_by_length are not part of the digest. They change embeddings only by about 1e-7, and including them would make the cache miss every time the batch size changed. A cached embedding is therefore the one computed the first time, whatever the batch size of later calls.

Use several threads and cores

threads: encoding

load_model(threads = ) sets how many threads the ONNX model uses to encode. threads = "auto" uses the number of performance cores on Apple Silicon and half the logical cores elsewhere. Encoding speeds up only up to the number of performance cores; more threads than that can make it slower.

model <- load_model("all-MiniLM-L6-v2", threads = "auto")
embeddings <- encode(abstracts$Abstract, model)

The number of threads never changes the embeddings.

cores: tokenizing, splitting, and comparing

cores is an argument of topics(), compare_topics(), topic_corpus(), coherence(), segment(), and topic_gamma(). With more than one core, these functions tokenize and split documents in parallel, and compare_topics() fits its topic counts in parallel.

prepared <- topic_corpus(abstracts$Abstract, embeddings = embeddings, cores = 4)
sweep <- compare_topics(prepared, n_topics = c(6, 8, 10, 12), cores = 4)

cores uses parallel::mclapply(), which works on Linux and macOS. On Windows, and for inputs of fewer than 2,000 texts, the work runs on one core, because starting extra processes would cost more than it saves.

Encoding sentences efficiently

Splitting documents into sentences multiplies the number of texts to encode. Two settings reduce that cost.

sort_by_length = TRUE encodes texts of similar length together. Every text in a batch is padded to the length of the longest one, so a batch of mixed lengths spends much of its time on padding. The more the lengths vary, as they do for sentences and clauses, the more this saves.

dedupe_segments = TRUE in topic_gamma() encodes each distinct sentence only once. How much it saves depends on how often sentences repeat in your corpus.

gamma <- topic_gamma(
  model_8, abstracts$Abstract,
  model = model,
  level = "sentence",
  sort_by_length = TRUE,
  dedupe_segments = TRUE,
  cores = 4
)

Both settings are off by default, because they change which texts share a batch and therefore move the embeddings by about 1e-7. That can, rarely, move a sentence that lies on the border between two topics.

The cheapest route is to fit the model on sentences in the first place. topics(segment = "sentence") splits, encodes, and stores every sentence with its abstract, so topic_gamma() needs no further encoding:

sentence_model <- topics(
  abstracts$Abstract,
  n_topics = 8,
  segment = "sentence",
  model = model,
  cores = 4
)
topic_gamma(sentence_model)

The static model

potion-base-8M is a static model: it looks up a vector for each word and averages them, without a neural network and without the ONNX Runtime. It encodes much faster than all-MiniLM-L6-v2, but it ignores word order. Whether its topics are as good depends on the corpus, so compare the two with compare_topics() before you switch.

fast <- load_model("potion-base-8M")
embeddings <- encode(abstracts$Abstract, fast)

Results do not depend on cores or threads

Tokenization is split by document and put back together in order, and every topic count is fitted independently, so cores never changes the result. The topic model itself uses no random numbers. The chunk below runs when the article is built: it fits the same model on one core and on four and compares the results. It uses random vectors in place of real embeddings, so it needs no download.

set.seed(1)
n <- 2500L
text <- paste(
  "document", seq_len(n),
  sample(c("alpha beta gamma", "delta epsilon zeta", "eta theta iota"), n, TRUE)
)
centers <- matrix(rnorm(8L * 64L), 8L, 64L)
embeddings <- centers[sample(8L, n, replace = TRUE), ] +
  matrix(rnorm(n * 64L, sd = 0.6), n, 64L)

one_core <- topics(text, n_topics = 6, embeddings = embeddings, cores = 1)
four_cores <- topics(text, n_topics = 6, embeddings = embeddings, cores = 4)

all.equal(terms(one_core), terms(four_cores))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(topic_sizes(one_core), topic_sizes(four_cores))
#> [1] TRUE

On Windows both fits run on one core, so the comparison is trivially true there.

Summary

  • Fitting several models to one corpus: pass embeddings, or use topic_corpus().
  • Running the same corpus again later: use encode(cache = ).
  • Encoding is slow: use load_model(threads = "auto"), or try the potion-base-8M model.
  • Large corpus on Linux or macOS: set cores.
  • Sentence-level models: use sort_by_length = TRUE, or fit with segment = "sentence".
  • Exact reproducibility: cores, threads, and cache never change results. Keep batch_size, sort_by_length, and dedupe_segments fixed once chosen.
